metaDescription: Six 1/2 HP sump pumps compared on cast iron versus thermoplastic, flow at lift, float design and warranty for wetter basements and longer discharge runs.
expertTake: The Wayne CDU800 is the 1/2 HP pump to buy for most wet basements, the Zoeller M98 is the premium cast iron choice for a pit you never want to think about, and the Lanchez 5200 GPH cast iron unit is the value gamble. Skip the 1/2 HP step if your pit is shallow and rarely fills, because 1/3 HP does the same job on less current and less money.
introParagraphs: Half a horsepower is where a sump pump stops being the default and starts being a decision. It buys real headroom for wetter pits and longer discharge lines, at the cost of a heavier startup draw and a higher price. The category also contains a wide spread of build quality, from cast iron units made for a decade of service to light thermoplastic pumps made for the shelf.

What matters in this size class is how the pump uses its extra power. A well-built 1/2 HP pump spends it on flow at height and on running cooler; a poorly built one spends it on a big number on the box. We rank them by housing, flow at real lift, float switch and the coverage behind them.

products.name: Wayne CDU800 1/2 HP cast iron submersible, 5,100 GPH
products.description:
The CDU800 combines a 1/2 HP motor, a cast iron and stainless steel body and a vertical float switch rated for one million cycles. Cast iron carries heat out of the motor into the pit water, and the vertical float travels in a narrow envelope so it fits older, tighter pits.

The cycle rating is the quiet selling point. Most manufacturers say nothing about switch life, and the switch is the part that most often leaves a basement flooded. A three-year warranty backs it. At 5,100 GPH it is rated well above the Superior 92572's 3,300 GPH at the same motor size, though both figures are zero-lift ratings.

The tradeoff is weight and price against thermoplastic options. For ownership, test the float quarterly, clean the screen twice a year and replace the check valve before it fails. In a house with a real water problem, this is the pump to start with. It also pairs well with a battery backup, because its vertical float leaves room beside it in a standard 18 inch pit for a second pump. Keep a spare check valve on the shelf, since the valve will wear out before the pump does.
products.bestFor: Wet basements and long discharge runs that need a proven cast iron pump.
pros: Float switch rated for a million cycles
Cast iron body cools the motor
cons: Zero-lift flow rating overstates real output
Needs a clean pit to avoid float hang-ups

products.name: Zoeller M98 Flow-Mate 1/2 HP cast iron sump pump
products.description:
The M98 is the premium 1/2 HP choice. An oil-filled motor sits inside a cast iron housing that, per its design, offers superior heat dissipation and so resists overheating. A vortex impeller keeps the spinning part out of the main flow path, and a snap-action float makes and breaks contact decisively.

A nine foot cord and an LED power plug make it easy to verify power at a glance, which is the kind of detail that saves a flashlight trip into the pit. It costs more than the Wayne CDU800 and does not list a higher flow rating, so you are paying for the vortex design and a long service record.

Ownership is plain. Keep the pit clean, check the float and valve yearly and expect many years of service. If the extra cost buys you peace of mind for a finished basement, it is justified. If you pull it every year for cleaning, handle it by the discharge pipe or a rope rather than the cord, and let the oil-filled motor cool before you reseat it.
products.bestFor: A finished basement where you want a proven vortex cast iron pump.
pros: Oil-filled motor in a cast iron body
cons: Costs more than the Wayne CDU800
No higher rated flow than cheaper rivals

products.name: Wayne SPF50 1/2 HP sump pump, 4,300 GPH
products.description:
The SPF50 is the honest-numbers pump of this group: 4,300 GPH at zero lift and 3,360 GPH at a stated height, a 22 percent drop. That second figure lets you check whether the pump will really keep up at your rise. The coated steel and thermoplastic body resists corrosion without the weight of iron.

A vertical float switch turns it on automatically and fits narrow pits. Compared with the CDU800 at 5,100 GPH, it rates lower at zero lift but gives you a real-world figure the Wayne iron pump does not publish in this data. Compared with the Superior 92572, it moves about a third more water on paper.

It is a solid mid-priced choice. Test the float, clean the screen and replace the check valve on a schedule. Its coated body resists chipping better than bare steel, and the vertical float makes it a clean drop-in for older pits.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want flow at lift, not just a maximum.
cons: Steel and plastic body cools less well than iron
Shorter record than the iron pumps

products.name: Lanchez 1/2 HP 5,200 GPH cast iron submersible pump
products.description:
The Lanchez 5200 pairs a 1/2 HP permanent split capacitor motor with a cast iron and stainless body and an integrated vertical float switch. A PSC motor is efficient and runs with a steady torque, and the iron body gives it the thermal advantage of the Wayne CDU800 at a lower cost.

Its 5,200 GPH rating is the highest in this group at zero lift, though that figure is a best case and the brand has less track record than Wayne or Zoeller. The vertical float fits narrow pits, and a cast iron body is a better long-term bet than thermoplastic.

Treat it as the value cast iron option. Check the warranty terms at purchase, test the float quarterly and replace the check valve on schedule. If it holds up, it saves a good sum over the premium brands. A fair rule with newer brands is to run it for a month, watch how it cycles, and test the float and check valve before the wet season arrives.
products.bestFor: A cast iron 1/2 HP pump on a tighter budget.
pros: Cast iron and stainless body at a lower cost
cons: Newer brand with less track record
Zero-lift rating is a best case

products.name: AQUASTRONG 1/2 HP sump pump 3,450 GPH stainless and cast iron
products.description:
The AQUASTRONG 3,450 GPH pump uses an adjustable float switch with a piggyback plug, so the float and pump plug into each other and into one outlet. The pump can also be run manually by plugging directly into the wall. A stainless steel and thermoplastic body with a cast iron volute gives a hybrid construction.

A 1-1/2 inch NPT discharge carries flow without as much friction as a 1 inch outlet. Compared with the Wayne CDU800 at 5,100 GPH, it moves about a third less on paper, and compared with the Lanchez 5200 it is a plainer, lighter machine.

The piggyback plug is convenient, but it is also a common failure point if the float cable is stressed. Inspect it each spring and keep the cord clear of the discharge pipe. Because the float and pump share a plug, a bad float cable can silence the pump, so test them together.
products.bestFor: A mid-priced pump with a detachable adjustable float.
pros: Cast iron volute in a hybrid body
cons: Lower rated flow than the iron pumps
Piggyback plug is a wear point

products.name: Superior Pump 92572 1/2 HP thermoplastic submersible pump
products.description:
The Superior 92572 is a thermoplastic 1/2 HP pump rated at 3,300 GPH and 25 feet of lift with a 10 foot cord and a vertical float. It is light, corrosion proof and affordable.

The plastic body does not shed heat like iron, so it suits pits with moderate duty rather than constant cycling. Its flow rating is about two thirds of the Wayne CDU800's, so it fits a wet but not flood-prone pit.

It is the budget brand pick. Test the float and clear the screen regularly, and treat it as a good spare if the primary is something heavier. It starts easily on a standard circuit and is light enough to swap in a few minutes if the primary ever fails.
products.bestFor: A moderate pit or a spare 1/2 HP pump at a low price.
cons: Plastic body sheds heat less well
Lower flow than the iron pumps

buyingCriteria.explanation: A 1/2 HP motor gives headroom over 1/3 HP for wetter pits and higher discharge. The Wayne CDU800 lists 5,100 GPH at zero lift and the Superior 92572 lists 3,300 GPH at the same motor size, so horsepower alone does not set flow. It also draws more at startup, so check the circuit. Use the motor size to judge startup amps and thermal margin, and use the pump curve to judge flow. A pit that fills a few inches in two minutes during a storm is a candidate for the bigger motor.

Cast iron sheds motor heat into the pit and holds up through long storm runs; the CDU800, M98 and Lanchez 5200 use it. Thermoplastic like the Superior 92572 is lighter and rust proof but runs hotter. Cast iron adds weight, so plan for a rope or handle when you pull the pump, and avoid dropping it on a concrete pit floor.

The Wayne SPF50 publishes 4,300 GPH at zero lift and 3,360 GPH at a stated height, a 22 percent drop. Use published curves, not maximums. To estimate your own lift, count the vertical feet from the pump to the pipe exit and add roughly a foot of equivalent head for every ten feet of straight pipe and for every elbow.

The float is the most common failure point. The CDU800's vertical float is rated for a million cycles; the AQUASTRONG's piggyback plug adds convenience and a wear point. Whatever you buy, test the float after any cord or pipe change, because that is when it tends to snag.

A 1-1/2 inch outlet, as on the AQUASTRONG, carries more flow than a 1 inch outlet with less friction. Match the pipe downstream. Do not reduce the pipe below the pump outlet, because a smaller pipe downstream throws away the benefit of a bigger motor.

A 1/2 HP pump pulls several times its running current at startup. Put it on a dedicated GFCI circuit and avoid sharing with a dehumidifier or freezer. A GFCI breaker can nuisance trip on damp pits, so choose a unit with an electrically sound plug and a clean cord.

specDecoder.meaning: Permanent split capacitor, an efficient single-phase design. It draws less current than an equivalent split phase design while staying quiet.
Oil carries heat from windings to the housing.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Zoeller M98 is oil filled in a cast iron case. Check oil-filled models for a sealed cap, since a leak means a failed seal.

specDecoder.meaning: How many on-off cycles the float is built to survive. A rating is not a guarantee, but it shows the maker designed the part to a cycle target.
The wet-end casing where the impeller spins. A cast iron volute resists the wear of fine silt for years.
specDecoder.watchFor: The AQUASTRONG uses cast iron for it.

specDecoder.meaning: Gallons per minute, GPH divided by 60. Use GPM to compare against the fill rate you measure in the pit.
specDecoder.watchFor: The SPF50 lists 72 GPM at zero lift.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cooling and body
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared cast iron, hybrid and thermoplastic builds. The CDU800, M98 and Lanchez 5200 lead. We also looked at whether the housing can be handled safely when pulled from the pit.

howWeEvaluated.title: Published flow
howWeEvaluated.description: We favored pumps that publish flow at two heights, like the SPF50's 4,300 and 3,360 GPH. Where a second flow figure was missing, we treated the maximum as a ceiling and said so.

howWeEvaluated.title: Float reliability
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed vertical floats, snap-action switches and piggyback plugs against failure modes. We counted a snap-action or rated switch as a plus because the float is the most common failure.

howWeEvaluated.title: Warranty and support
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered the three-year coverage on the CDU800 against pumps with no stated term. A pump with a clear warranty and parts supply scored above one with none.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared price tier with build rather than rewarding the lowest cost or highest rated flow. We checked that no pump was ranked above its tier on a single flow number.

cards.label: Cast iron
cards.text: The CDU800, M98 and Lanchez 5200 cool the motor better and last longer in long storm runs.

cards.label: Thermoplastic
cards.text: The Superior 92572 and SPF50 are lighter and cheaper but run warmer.

howToChoose.note: Cast iron for a primary; plastic for moderate duty.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Cast iron, a rated float and a 1-1/2 inch discharge. A wet basement runs the pump for hours.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Wayne CDU800 and Zoeller M98 meet that standard; the Lanchez 5200 GPH does so at lower cost.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: The basement is finished or the pit has flooded. The M98 or CDU800 justify their cost.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: The pit is shallow. The Superior 92572 is enough.

maintenance.why: Confirm the pump starts and stops. A stuck float is the usual failure. Do it again after any long power outage.
Silt chokes the intake and raises motor heat. Rinse it with clean water and check that the impeller spins freely.
Backflow causes short cycling. Replace it before the wet season, not after a failure.
Damaged insulation is a hazard. Look at the strain relief where the cord enters the motor.
Gravel and sludge jam floats. A clean pit keeps the float and impeller free.

faq.a: It has more headroom for wet pits and long discharge, but draws more at startup. For an average basement, 1/3 HP is enough. Time how fast your pit fills before deciding, and size for the worst storm you have seen.

faq.q: Do I need cast iron at 1/2 HP?
faq.a: For a primary pump in a wet basement, yes. Cast iron cools the motor better. For moderate duty, thermoplastic is acceptable. Cast iron also lasts longer in pits that cycle often.

faq.q: What circuit does a 1/2 HP pump need?
faq.a: A dedicated GFCI circuit is best practice. The startup surge can trip a shared breaker. Ask an electrician if you are unsure about the circuit.

faq.q: Why does the rating say 5,100 GPH but my pump moves less?
faq.a: The rating is at zero lift. Real flow falls as the water rises, so read the curve. Use the published curve if the maker provides one.

faq.q: How long should a 1/2 HP pump last?
faq.a: Several years, depending on cycling. Cast iron units last longer. Check the check valve and float, because they fail more often than motors.
It is convenient but a wear point. Inspect it each spring. Replace the plug if the cable looks stressed or the insulation cracks.
